passage:
Shift supervisor's note, Friday, café team
Two of my trainees handled today's order mix-up very differently. A table of eight got the wrong food because the order slip was smudged in the rain and the printer was down.
Pankaj apologised to the customers, then to me, then to the cook, then again at closing. He said, 'It's all my fault, I ruin everything.' He had written the order correctly.
Rekha said the cook can't read, the printer is junk and the customers mumbled. She had skipped reading the order back, which is our rule.
What I did next: I sat with each of them separately, and we drew a line down a napkin, my part and not my part. Pankaj's column was nearly empty. Rekha's had one clear line: read the order back. Both looked surprised. I will check in with them next week.

qa.q: Why did the table of eight get the wrong food?
qa.a: The order slip was smudged in the rain and the printer was down.

qa.q: What does Pankaj saying 'I ruin everything' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels heavy guilt and takes on blame for things he didn't cause, since he had written the order correctly.

qa.q: What choice did the supervisor make after the shift, and how did it help both trainees?
qa.a: The supervisor sat with each one separately to split 'my part' from 'not my part', showing Pankaj his column was nearly empty and Rekha that reading back was hers.

qa.q: How might the cook feel hearing Rekha say the cook can't read?
qa.a: The cook might feel hurt and unfairly blamed, since the slip was smudged and the missing step was Rekha's.

grounding: Shows one young adult blaming himself for everything and another blaming everyone else, and an adult helping each separate their own part from circumstances.

passage:
Sunday night
Irfan quit the band today, two days before the fest. Of course my first thought: it's my fault. I picked the second song. I booked the practice room for 7 a.m. I should have noticed he was tired.
I spent the whole afternoon drafting apology messages. Deleted every one.
Then I called Nani, and she asked a question that stung: 'Did you make him leave, or did he decide?'
He decided. He told Joel it was because he has a job interview on Tuesday. Nothing to do with the song or the room.
My part, honestly: I didn't ask anyone before booking the 7 a.m. slot. I can own that and say sorry to the group for that one thing.
The rest is his choice, and his life.
Minakshi

qa.q: Why did Irfan tell Joel he was leaving the band?
qa.a: Because he has a job interview on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling while drafting apology messages all afternoon?
qa.a: Minakshi felt guilty, believing Irfan's leaving was Minakshi's fault because of the song and the early practice slot.

qa.q: What question changed things for Minakshi, and what did Minakshi decide next?
qa.a: Nani's question about whether Irfan was made to leave or decided helped Minakshi see only the 7 a.m. booking was Minakshi's part, and to apologise for that alone.

qa.q: How might the rest of the band see Minakshi's apology about the 7 a.m. slot?
qa.a: They may find one clear, specific apology easier to accept than a flood of guilt, and feel their own views on the timing were heard.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking on guilt for a bandmate's choice and then separating their own small part from what was the bandmate's decision.

passage: Counsellor's note, drop-in hour. Pema, second year, came in because she can't stop feeling guilty that her friend Ira dropped out and went home. "If I'd studied with her more, she'd have stayed." She has said versions of this for three weeks. I asked her to draw a circle and list everything that went into Ira's choice. She wrote: Ira's family's money trouble, Ira's health, Ira's own wish to change courses, and, small at the edge, "I was busy in October." She sat looking at it. "That's a very small piece," she said. Next step: we will meet again on Thursday, and she will call Ira just to talk, not to apologise.

qa.q: What did Pema write small at the edge of the circle?
qa.a: "I was busy in October."

qa.q: What has Pema been feeling for three weeks?
qa.a: She has felt guilty and responsible for Ira's decision to drop out.

qa.q: Why did the circle exercise help?
qa.a: It separated Pema's small part from Ira's family, health and own wishes, giving a more balanced view.

qa.q: How might Ira feel getting a call just to talk?
qa.a: Ira would likely feel cared for, not burdened by an apology for something that wasn't Pema's fault.

grounding: Shows a young adult taking on guilt for a friend's choice and learning to separate her part from circumstances.

passage:
Friday. Failed the circuits exam. My first thoughts: the professor sets impossible papers, Siddharth didn't share his notes in time, and the hostel was too noisy. I told everyone that at dinner. Siddharth said, quietly, "I sent you the notes two weeks ago, Wasim." I checked. He had. I hadn't opened them. That shut me up. So, trying to be honest here: the paper was hard, that's true, and the hostel is noisy. But I skipped four classes and started studying two nights before. That part's mine. It feels worse to write that than to blame people. It also feels like something I can actually fix.
Wasim

qa.q: How many classes did Wasim skip?
qa.a: Four classes.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel after checking the notes?
qa.a: Wasim felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, realising the blame had been unfair.

qa.q: What balanced view does Wasim reach?
qa.a: That the hard paper and noise were real, but skipping classes and late studying were Wasim's own part to fix.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt being blamed at dinner?
qa.a: Siddharth was probably hurt and annoyed, having sent the notes two weeks earlier.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who blames everyone else, then separates their own part from the circumstances.

passage:
In their small town near Nashik, Pankaj and Sumit shared a room above the tailor's shop while doing their diplomas.
When Pankaj's younger brother dropped out of college, Pankaj didn't sleep for a week. "It's my fault. I should have called him more. I should have sent money." His guilt was everywhere, even though his brother had decided alone.
Sumit, meanwhile, failed his electrical practical. "The examiner hated me. The equipment was rubbish. My partner was useless." He never once looked at his own preparation.
One evening their landlady, Kamala Tai, heard both of them grumbling. "Pankaj, your brother made his own choice. You can call him now; you can't choose for him. Sumit, the equipment was old, yes. But did you practise the wiring?"
Sumit went quiet. Pankaj, for the first time that week, breathed out.

qa.q: What did Sumit fail?
qa.a: His electrical practical.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel about his brother dropping out?
qa.a: He felt deeply guilty and blamed himself, not sleeping for a week, even though his brother decided alone.

qa.q: How did Kamala Tai help both young men see things in a balanced way?
qa.a: She told Pankaj his brother's choice was his brother's own, and asked Sumit about his own practice, helping each separate his own part from the circumstances.

qa.q: What would change if Sumit looked at his own preparation?
qa.a: He might see what he could do differently, like practising the wiring, instead of blaming others and never changing.

grounding: Shows one young man overblaming himself for another's choice and his roommate blaming everyone else, and an adult helping each separate his own part.
